Messages.Author: echia...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
I can sympathize with your situation.

Several years back, with the old qualifying rules (no ties for
qualifying spots), I was in a 3-way tie for 2 qualifier spots. We had
to roll a dice and, suffice it to say, I rolled the lowest among the
3. (That really sucked).

I was really pleased when years later, they changed to allow for ties
in Qualifying spots (though that still sometimes creates hassles when
there aren't enough t-shirts).

- Regarding ties for the actual finals, I don't think there's really a
better way to do it. When you get to the point where even Tournament
Points are tied, you're going to be splitting hairs regardless of what
method you choose. There's sufficient randomness in the game that you
really can't compare the performance of the other players (besides
through TP's in that game). So the die roll is the simplest and
fastest.

- Regarding the qualifying spots, I do think you make a good argument
on why they should alter the rules so that those who tied for a finals
spot (but lost on the dice roll) would still qualify. I really don't
think it's a big deal from an organizational standpoint, since over
the past few years, they have gradually been relaxing the qualifying
standards (to broaden participation). Allowing local mini-qualifiers,
giving automatic qualifying spots for organizers, automatic
qualification for those in the continental finals from the previous
year, etc. It shouldn't be a problem to also have an allowance for
people who just barely lost out on the finals due to the dice roll.

Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:
On Mon, 16 Nov 2009 23:19:41 -0800 (PST), Acbishop
<antonio_c...@hotmail.com> wrote:

> I finished 5th place the EC last Sunday tied with Kamel, and I lost
> the dice roll to get a place in the finals :(
>
> And even worse, aparently only the finalists of previous Continental
> championship and not the first five people of the previous are
> qualified for the next one. I can understand that for playing the
> final it should be a way of determining the finalist, but in
> qualifiers tournaments people tied with the last spot get also
> qualified for the next EC, why could it be fare not to be qualified
> for next EC when I finished within the first 5 people(tied) after the
> 3 rounds of Day 2 of the EC?

Finalists qualify. Or the first five people qualify. You ended up being
6th place; there are four 2nd place and one 1st place players.

> So the dice roll rules on that as well?

Dice (coins, etc.) are used as a tie-breaker. Unless something better
tournament-specific performance indicator can be used (e.g. counting
pool you have left at the end of each game, etc.), I don't see an
alternative to randomization.

> Why not implement a systï¿œme which calculates as wells the points that

> people in your tables did to have any other way of avoidings ties like
> ELO system in other cardgames?

Because such "systï¿œme" would suck. If you introduce a pre-condition that
has nothing to do with performance at the given tournament (e.g. the
ELO or some ranking) then not only do you put an extra pressure on the
people processing the results (I can imagine a similar whine-post on
losing the ELO-based tie-breaker because a previous tournament result
wasn't processed), but you are not necessarily being any more fair
than with the 50/50 randomness.

If you use something at the tournament... You don't get a guarantee of
fairness. Assume a 50-player tournament with two hubs. First hub
contains world-class players as opponents, second hub contains noobs
as opponents. Getting the same result (e.g. 2 GW 6 VP) from each hub
will carry a completely different set of difficulty. Even the 50/50
randomization is more fair in this case than to say that the guy
scoring 2/6 in the noob hub had a more difficult set of adversaries
(if they happen to score better).

I really hate the randomization. I just don't see an alternative to it.
Going beneath TPs would create artificial criteria that would introduce
more book-keeping, more calculations, and not necessarily be any more
fair (TPs are a borderline case, even they are pretty artificial, and
serve only as tie-breakers - but do they really track performance? Is
it really a "better" loss to lose to a single opponent than to lose to
two opponents who potentially table-split? etc.).

Random tie-breakers, while unfair when applied, have a generally
beneficial side too - they remove the tactical element from the game
that aspires to exploit whatever favorable pre-condition the player
may be subject to, and instead urges everyone to achieve as many GWs
and VPs as possible.

--
Regards,

Daneel

Messages.Author: echia...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:
On Nov 17, 7:56 pm, Brum <tiago.br...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I think the real problem here is to Qualify to a Final (or even a
> Win).
> Also, lets not forget the qualification for tournaments of limited
> number of players, like 2nd day EC or NAC.
>
> I don't know how it works, but could the Archon order between players
> through "quality of ousts"?
> For instance, when in tie, the player that ousted the better players
> wins.
> Could this bring any extra problems?

I think the main challenge is that systems that work well in 2-player
games don't port over quite as well in multi-player (4 or 5-player)
ones. In a two-player game (i.e. MtG) the quality of defeated
opponents does make some sense (because you win largely on your own
merits). But in VTES, I don't think it's as useful. You'd have to keep
careful notes of table seating and order of ousts (if B ousts C but
then A ousts B, does the transitive property apply with A being a
better player than C?). Also, the political dynamic really alters
things as well. If anything, a lot of the the best players (or the
ones with the best decks) may be seen as the table threat and everyone
else may try to oust him. Alternatively, there may be times when you
get your predator or grandprey ousted on purpose, etc. None of that is
reflected by the quality of ousts, which is why I think it would be a
poor system to implement.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija
Messages.Body:
On Nov 17, 9:28 pm, Brum <tiago.br...@gmail.com> wrote:
> But the randomness of dice is just... too random.

It is. This is true. But *all* tie breakers eventually end with "well,
we have to flip a coin, then". You can split and parse and split all
day long, but eventually, you are still going to end up with a tied
tie. And the only way to break the tied tie (or tied tied tied tie) is
random selection (well, that, or feat of strength, but there is only
so far that is going to get you...). As it stands, we have 3 levels of
ranking/tie breaking--GW/VP/TP. *Most* of the time, there is enough
differentiaton that you don't need to flip a coin. Every once and a
while, you do. If there was a 4th level of tie breaking, still, every
once and a while, you'd need to flip a coin. Sure, it sucks. But it is
really the only reasonable way to go about things.

-Peter

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"Brum" <tiago...@gmail.com> wrote in message news:3c166295-fe13-447b...@g23g2000yqh.googlegroups.com...

> But the randomness of dice is just... too random.

What are you going to do, though? The randomness of tournament points
is just too random for my blood. The whole concept is silly. TPs don't
begin to measure the quality of how a player played a tournament. They're
just a static version of rolling the die. On top of this, you want a
_different_ static version of rolling the die?

I'd question whether such systems are a good thing. In theory, they
allow players to predict whether they'd qualify for finals in a given
set of circumstances ("Joe on table 5 gets his oust before being ousted
by his predator whereas I win this table with 2 1/2 victory points;
would I get in or not?") which is actually not good because it might
encourage people to play games with their tournament standing in
mind. That is, it's OK to play with the mindset that, "The better I
do in this game, the better chance I'll have to make the finals." But
my understanding of the play-to-win rule is that it's NOT OK to play
with the goal that (for instance) "1 1/2 VPs gets me into the finals
but only 1 does not".

To that end, I think it's actually better to leave it to a die roll,
the result of which cannot be predicted until it takes place.

Fred

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"librarian" <auct...@superfuncards.com> wrote in message news:he13i1$pqn$3...@news.eternal-september.org...

> Peter D Bakija wrote:
> Math people, help me out - my feeling is that at larger tournaments, you are more likely to have a tie, since there will be more
> people with exact same results. And of course at a larger tournament, it feels worse to decide something like who is in the
> finals on a coin flip.

I think it would depend on the statistical curve. That is, to make the top
5 out of 12 is a different thing than making the top 5 out of 80. Of
necessity, the top 5 out of 80 will have won more victory points and
probably be less likely to land on exactly the same number of VPs and TPs.
On the other hand, the effect you cite matters, too. I don't know which
one would matter more. But my point is, it's not just the number of
people - it's also what position on the curve is one that matters for
breaking ties. (If there's a tie between three people for third place,
it would get broken but we wouldn't care that much about it. If there's
a tie for 12th place, we wouldn't care about it unless it's where the
qualification line stood. And with current rules, I'm hearing that it
wouldn't get broken anyway.)

Also, keep in mind: with more people, organizers tend to plan longer
tournaments. Three rounds provides more results than two round so there
will be fewer ties for that (indirect) reason.

Fred

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:
> That is, it's OK to play with the mindset that, "The better I
> do in this game, the better chance I'll have to make the finals." But
> my understanding of the play-to-win rule is that it's NOT OK to play
> with the goal that (for instance) "1 1/2 VPs gets me into the finals
> but only 1 does not".

PTW means that you play for the 1.5 VPs instead of the 1 VP for no other reason
than 1.5 > 1 (it has nothing to do with the finals).

PTW:

Play to get the best result reasonably possible for yourself.

Order of results:
1 GW
0 GW and 2 VP
0 GW and 1.5 VP
0 GW and 1 VP
0 GW and 0 VP

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote in message
news:he178s$kff$1...@news.eternal-september.org...

> Frederick Scott wrote:
>> That is, it's OK to play with the mindset that, "The better I
>> do in this game, the better chance I'll have to make the finals." But
>> my understanding of the play-to-win rule is that it's NOT OK to play
>> with the goal that (for instance) "1 1/2 VPs gets me into the finals
>> but only 1 does not".
>
> PTW means that you play for the 1.5 VPs instead of the 1 VP for no other reason
> than 1.5 > 1 (it has nothing to do with the finals).
>
> PTW:
>
> Play to get the best result reasonably possible for yourself.

Sure. I think the reason this is an issue has to do with evaluating scenarios
where a player is making value judgements between, say, a high chance of
finishing with 1.5 VPs (in the above scenario) vs. a smaller chance of going
for 2 VP or more and taking the game win.

Of course, neither strictly violates play-to-win, as the player is left to his
own devices in sorting out such priorities. I'm just saying that the value of
the rule, in my humble opinion, is to keep the opportunities for each game more
equal to all the players involved. So it doesn't have to matter to another
player - who may need a game win and a sweep to make the finals - whether he's
seated in a game where there's one or more people who are merely trying to get
a victory point or so and then sit on their positions rather than being seated
at a table of four other players who all feel they need to go for game wins.
The latter would certainly provide the easier opportunity to sweep.

You said it yourself: playing to get the best result reasonably possible for
yourself has nothing to do with the finals - which was my point.

Fred
